solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Peculiar rite with this armour leads to "requiescat in pieces"

indicators.note: something in pieces has been broken up, so the Latin word's letters are to be put back together differently
the odd rite is the part of the jumble that is set aside, leaving only the armour's letters behind

blocks.note: Latin for 'may he rest', as on a tombstone; the whole jumble
taken as written; these letters come out of the jumble

explanation.surface: A strange funeral rite in which someone's armour ends up smashed to bits, rest in peace.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: RITE plus CASQUE, jumbled, makes REQUIESCAT, so take RITE's letters out of REQUIESCAT and rearrange the rest. The joke is on 'requiescat in pace'.
explanation.definitionFit: A casque is a helmet, a piece of head armour, so 'this armour' points at the answer itself.

clue.text: Baltic brass's sassy stance

indicators.note: sassy means cheeky and unruly, so the following word's letters misbehave and fall out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheeky posture adopted by some bigwigs from the Baltic states.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' looks like top officials, but it is slang for money: centas were coins of Lithuania, a Baltic state, before the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: Centas is the plural of centas, the former Lithuanian hundredth-of-a-litas coin, and brass is British slang for cash.

clue.text: Fish to do for August, no sign of umming and ahhing

indicators.note: having no sign of something means it is absent, so the hesitation sound is taken out of the verb

blocks.note: to do for something is to ruin or wreck it
the hesitation noise a speaker makes while dithering
the month's standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone decisively plans to ruin August with fish, without dithering.
explanation.walkthrough: SCUPPER loses its ER, then the month's abbreviation follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The scuppaug is a North American fish, the porgy or scup, a food fish of the Atlantic coast.

clue.text: Query not entirely to Persian dynasty

blocks.note: Q is the standard abbreviation for query
a door pushed to is closed; one not fully to is ajar

explanation.surface: Someone queries whether something has not quite reached the old Persian royal house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' reads as a preposition, but it is the adverb in 'pull the door to', meaning shut; a door not entirely shut is ajar.
explanation.definitionFit: The Qajars were the Turkic ruling house of Iran from 1789 to 1925, so their name is the dynasty's.

clue.text: Slip by east end of chapel and part of choir

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only the last one of the building is kept

blocks.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east
the last letter of chapel
the apse is the rounded recess at the east end of a church, beyond the choir

explanation.surface: Someone slips past the east end of the chapel and into part of the choir stalls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slip by' looks like a person sneaking past, but it is the verb for time passing.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that elapses slips by or passes, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Such form of helping Mark to the van gets you doing as Abigail does?

indicators.note: the van is the front, so the mark is the extra front letter that must be removed to leave the answer

blocks.note: M is a standard abbreviation for mark
an abigail is a lady's maid, so what she does is maiding

explanation.surface: A mark placed at the front of a form for a helper, and a question about what Abigail does.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: put M in front of the answer and you get MAIDING. Abigail, from a maid in a 17th-century play, is a dated word for a lady's maid.
explanation.definitionFit: Aiding is the present participle of aid, so it is one grammatical form of the verb helping.

clue.text: Tense from a profit but that which gets one going for good

indicators.note: one thing going for another means it takes the other's place, so a letter is swapped

blocks.note: taken as written
grist to the mill is something turned to profit
the first letter, the one that gets the word going
the letter O, shaped like a ring, is often clued as one
G is the standard abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Someone is anxious about profit, but finds something that gets them going for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grist to the mill' is anything turned to profit. 'One going for good' tells you the ring-shaped letter for one takes the place of the abbreviation for good.
explanation.definitionFit: The aorist is a past tense of Greek verbs expressing simple action, so it is a grammatical tense.

clue.text: Plant one limey over each

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
both are slang for a Brit, limey in America and pom in Australia
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
EA is the standard abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: A single Englishman planted over each, as if posting a sentry.
explanation.walkthrough: A limey is American slang for a Briton, and pom the Australian equivalent.
explanation.definitionFit: Ipomoea is the genus of climbing plants that includes morning glory and the sweet potato.

clue.text: One shining brightly in earlier prayer day is upset

indicators.note: in a down clue an upset thing is turned upside down, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: bene is an obsolete word for a prayer, hence 'earlier'
D is the standard abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: Someone notices that a day earlier, during prayers, something shining was knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earlier' marks the old sense: bene, as in Wordsworth, is an archaic word for prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: Deneb is the brightest star in Cygnus, the Swan, and one of the brightest in the sky.

clue.text: Denials Unionist Liberal included in dismissal? Sadly not

indicators.note: something included in another sits inside it, so the party abbreviation goes within the dismissal

blocks.note: noes, refusals, written as nos
U is the abbreviation for Unionist
getting the chuck is being dismissed or jilted
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A Unionist and a Liberal both deny being involved in a sacking, and it seems that is untrue.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the Liberal is included in the dismissal; the Unionist simply follows the denials. To get the chuck is British slang for being sacked.
explanation.definitionFit: 'No such luck' is the idiom said when a hope is disappointed, meaning unfortunately it did not happen.

clue.text: Scots savoury — it'll be seconds for Fink-Nottle, and others

indicators.note: saying one thing will be another tells you a letter of the Scots word changes into a different one

blocks.note: gustie is a Scots word meaning tasty or savoury
S is the standard abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: A Scottish savoury dish that everyone, Fink-Nottle included, will have second helpings of.
explanation.walkthrough: The T of GUSTIE (time, read as 'it' in the surface) becomes S for seconds. Gussie Fink-Nottle is the newt-loving friend of Bertie Wooster in P G Wodehouse's stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Gussie is a pet form of Augustus, borne by Wodehouse's Fink-Nottle and by other people so named.

clue.text: At liberty to check lines round shell-like?

indicators.note: to check something is to hold it in, so the freed word contains the other letters

blocks.note: one who has escaped is at liberty
L is an abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural
O is a round shape

explanation.surface: Someone at liberty is told to check the lines around something that looks like a shell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shell-like' is British slang for an ear, as in 'a word in your shell-like', but here it means literally shaped like a shell.
explanation.definitionFit: Escalloped is a variant of scalloped, cut or shaped with the wavy edge of a scallop shell.

clue.text: A short top, for example, rising on prize supper

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read upwards, so the abbreviation is turned round

blocks.note: a cotta is a short surplice, a garment worn on top
the usual abbreviation for 'for example'
a pie, as in a share of the pie, is a prize to be divided up

explanation.surface: A cropped top, say, gets a lift from winning a prize supper.
explanation.walkthrough: A cotta is a short white surplice worn by clergy and choristers.
explanation.definitionFit: Cottage pie, minced beef topped with mashed potato, is a classic British family supper dish.

clue.text: Being noble somebody is filling cakes

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something, so the phrase goes within the cakes

blocks.note: cakes of soap or chocolate come as bars
one's, short for one is, with one meaning somebody

explanation.surface: Being a person of quality, somebody is putting the filling into cakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being noble' reads as a participle phrase, but it is a noun: a being who is noble.
explanation.definitionFit: A baroness is a woman holding the lowest rank of the peerage, so she is a noble person.

clue.text: Hummer to reverse move quickly

indicators.note: to reverse something is to run it backwards, so the move is spelt right to left

blocks.note: taken as written
to zap is to move or go very fast

explanation.surface: An instruction to put a large army vehicle into reverse quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hummer looks like the military truck; it is a hummingbird, and the topaz is a South American hummingbird.
explanation.definitionFit: Hummingbirds are called hummers from the sound of their wings, and the topaz is one such bird.

clue.text: From which one selects fellows oneself

blocks.note: fellows are men
us used for the speaker, as in 'give us a kiss'

explanation.surface: A self-selection process in which one chooses fellows like oneself.
explanation.walkthrough: In dialect and casual speech us stands for me, the speaker themself.
explanation.definitionFit: Menus are lists of dishes or options that a diner or computer user picks from.

clue.text: A page concerned with lock is being printed

indicators.note: to be concerned with something is to be involved in it, so the letter goes inside

blocks.note: taken as written
a tress is a lock of hair
P is the standard abbreviation for page

explanation.surface: A page boy involved with a lock is being printed in a news story.
explanation.walkthrough: P goes inside TRESS after its first letter, with A in front.
explanation.definitionFit: A book at press is in the process of being printed, so the phrase means going through the press.

clue.text: Fuss for Falkirkers also aboard steamship over swing to the left

indicators.note: something aboard a ship is inside it, so the word for also goes within the vessel's letters

blocks.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship
too means also
hie is a call to a horse to turn to the left

explanation.surface: A row among people from Falkirk aboard a steamer about a political lurch leftwards.
explanation.walkthrough: Falkirk is a Scottish town, so the definition is the Scots word. In a down clue 'over' puts the ship before the call.
explanation.definitionFit: Stooshie is a Scots word for a commotion, row or fuss, used by people from places like Falkirk.

clue.text: Main Street with pollarded tree

indicators.note: a pollarded tree has had its top cut off, so the first letter of the tree is removed

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
the maple is a tree

explanation.surface: A main street lined with trees cut back hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main Street' reads as one name, but Main is the definition and Street gives the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A staple product or food is the principal or chief one, so main is an adjectival synonym.

clue.text: Rows about Northern Ireland's sheds locally

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the rows wrap around the Ulster abbreviation

blocks.note: rows are lines
NI is the abbreviation for Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Arguments break out over Northern Ireland's huts and outbuildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rows' wants to be quarrels, but it means lines. 'Locally' marks a dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: A linny or linhay is a dialect word for an open-fronted farm shed, so linnies are sheds.

clue.text: Cut support by French char

blocks.note: a tee supports a golf ball
thé is French for tea, and char is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: A cut to support given by a French charwoman.
explanation.walkthrough: Char looks like a cleaner or burnt food, but it is British slang for tea, from Chinese cha.
explanation.definitionFit: A teething baby is cutting teeth, and 'cut' in this sense means to grow them through the gums.

clue.text: I'm hired to greet leader of Israelites, one ending in suicide

indicators.note: an ending is the final letter of a word, so just the last one of the final word is kept

blocks.note: Saul was the first king of Israel
the Roman numeral for one
the last letter of suicide

explanation.surface: Someone hired to welcome the Israelite king, one who died by suicide.
explanation.walkthrough: Greet is Scots for weep, so the definition is a paid mourner. Saul fell on his own sword, which ties the surface together.
explanation.definitionFit: A saulie is a Scots word for a hired mourner at a funeral, a person paid to weep.

clue.text: To wit, bloody millions in race

blocks.note: sc is the abbreviation for scilicet, Latin for namely or to wit
a raw wound is bloody
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: That is to say, a fortune is spent in a cut-throat contest.
explanation.walkthrough: Race here is the old verb (also spelt rase) meaning to scratch, not a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrawm is a dialect verb meaning to scratch, and race in its obsolete sense also meant to scratch or graze.

clue.text: City of sculpture, say, modified covers over wings

indicators.note: modified means changed, so the letters of the craft are rearranged

blocks.note: Ely is the cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
sculpture is an example of art

explanation.surface: A city known for its sculpture, which has been altered by roofing over its wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wings' suggests a building's wings, but they are a beetle's.
explanation.definitionFit: Elytra are a beetle's hardened forewings, which form sheaths covering the delicate flying wings beneath.

clue.text: Dash about after American in oily ploy

indicators.note: oily suggests something slippery that slides about, so the letters are moved into a new order

blocks.note: a is short for about, from circa
A is the abbreviation for American
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sprint around after an American who is caught up in a slippery trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dash' looks like a sprint, but in West African English a dash is a tip or bribe.
explanation.definitionFit: Payola is a secret bribe, especially to a DJ to play a record, and a dash is a West African bribe.

clue.text: Whenever leaving dummy becomes smarter

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so those letters are taken out of the baby's dummy

blocks.note: if can mean whenever, as in 'if it rains, I stay in'
pacifier is the American word for a baby's dummy

explanation.surface: Whenever a baby gives up the dummy, it becomes more grown up.
explanation.walkthrough: A dummy is the British word for a baby's rubber teat, known in America as a pacifier.
explanation.definitionFit: Smart can mean brisk, as in a smart pace, so smarter and pacier both mean faster.

clue.text: She makes good acting with tense and heavy blow

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for acting, as in an acting post
T is the grammarians' abbreviation for tense
a oner is a single heavy blow

explanation.surface: An actress makes good, performing tensely and delivering a heavy blow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' is not a woman in the scene but any person who makes amends.
explanation.definitionFit: To make good a wrong is to atone for it, so one who does so is an atoner.

clue.text: Trim and uniform unisex wrap

blocks.note: to pare is to trim
Uniform is the radio code word for U

explanation.surface: A tailor's instruction to trim a uniform and make a garment for either sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trim and uniform' reads like a smart outfit, but each word gives a separate piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A pareu is a Polynesian length of cloth worn wrapped round the body by both men and women.

clue.text: Tear a strip off wood dressed by lumpkin

indicators.note: something dressed by another is clothed in it, so the clumsy fellow wraps around the wood

blocks.note: a lumpkin is a clumsy oaf, a lout
ash is a timber

explanation.surface: A clumsy oaf rips a strip from a plank of wood he has dressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear a strip off' looks literal, but it is the British idiom for scolding someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To lash out at someone is to attack them verbally, much as tearing a strip off them is a fierce rebuke.

clue.text: Outburst of delight then disgust finding meadow in Moray

blocks.note: ha is an exclamation of pleasure or triumph
ugh is a cry of disgust

explanation.surface: Someone cries out in delight, then disgust, on finding a field in north-east Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Moray is a Scottish region, which flags a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: A haugh is a Scots word for a stretch of flat riverside land, a water meadow.

clue.text: Fieldwork nurtured a non-specialist to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so only a part of the run of words is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the ends of the first three words

explanation.surface: Someone describes how they raised a generalist, in part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fieldwork' wants to be research in the field, but it is a military field fortification.
explanation.definitionFit: A redan is a V-shaped field fortification with two faces forming a salient angle, so it is a fieldwork.

clue.text: Asian barge business that's steady but for husband and wife

indicators.note: but for means except, so those letters are left out of the steady earner

blocks.note: a cash cow is a business that brings in a steady income
H is the abbreviation for husband
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: An Asian barge business that would be a steady earner if it were not for the married couple running it.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the two spouses' abbreviations out of CASHCOW.
explanation.definitionFit: A casco is a Philippine lighter or barge, so it is a type of Asian cargo boat.

clue.text: Athletic beauty, well, one backing what whets the whistle

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the word for healthy is read from right to left

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for athletic, as in AAA
a peri is a fairy of Persian myth, a beautiful being
a fit one is a well one, healthy

explanation.surface: A sporty beauty, well, someone going backwards, has the drink that gets things going.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'whet the appetite' is mixed with 'wet the whistle', meaning have a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperitif is an alcoholic drink taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite.

clue.text: Porter, say, with lost genius lifting gizmo for draughts

blocks.note: porter is a dark beer
engine is an obsolete word for genius or ingenuity

explanation.surface: A railway porter who has lost his touch, raising a device for a board game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draughts' looks like the board game, called checkers in America; it means draught beer. 'Lost' flags the obsolete sense of engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A beer engine is the hand pump on a bar that draws draught beer up from the cellar.

clue.text: This petrified Dutch trapped in tableland

indicators.note: something trapped in another is held inside it, so the abbreviation sits within the tableland

blocks.note: a mesa is a flat-topped hill or plateau
DU is an abbreviation for Dutch

explanation.surface: A Dutchman is frozen with fear after getting stuck on a plateau.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Petrified' looks like frightened, but it is literal: Medusa turned people to stone.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Medusa the Gorgon turned anyone who looked at her into stone.

clue.text: Once again judge is stern about grunt of surprise

indicators.note: about means around, so the stern surrounds the noise

blocks.note: the stern is the rear of a ship
eh is an exclamation of surprise or query

explanation.surface: Again a judge is stern, grunting in surprise at the case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stern' looks like an adjective for the judge, but it is the back of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehear a case is to judge it a second time, giving it a fresh hearing.
